blocks.content: This is the single most useful topic for tying everything in this module together: what actually happens, step by step, between you typing docker run nginx and a container being alive on your machine.
1. You Type the Command

Everything starts with the client. The docker CLI parses docker run nginx, figuring out which image you want, what options you passed (ports, environment variables, volumes), and what API call this needs to become.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784479579308-958471495.png
blocks.alt: The CLI first has to parse what you asked for

blocks.content: 2. The Request Reaches the Daemon

The client packages that parsed command into a REST API request and sends it over the Unix socket to the daemon. From this point forward, the client is essentially just waiting for a response to display to you, it is the daemon doing every remaining step.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784479580941-876339046.png
blocks.alt: From here on, the daemon is driving

blocks.content: 3. Does the Daemon Already Have the Image?
blocks.text: 3. Does the Daemon Already Have the Image?

blocks.content: The daemon first checks whether nginx already exists in its local image cache. If it is already there from a previous pull, the daemon skips straight to creating the container. If not, it reaches out to the configured registry (Docker Hub, by default) and pulls the image first.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784479582475-944322335.png
blocks.alt: A cache hit skips the registry entirely

blocks.content:
docker images | grep nginx
# If this shows a result, "docker run nginx" will not
# touch the network at all, it uses the cached image directly.

code.content:
docker images | grep nginx
# If this shows a result, "docker run nginx" will not
# touch the network at all, it uses the cached image directly.

codes.bash:
docker images | grep nginx
# If this shows a result, "docker run nginx" will not
# touch the network at all, it uses the cached image directly.

blocks.content: 4. The Daemon Delegates the Actual Execution
blocks.text: 4. The Daemon Delegates the Actual Execution

blocks.content: With an image ready, the daemon does not directly spin up the process itself. It hands the job to containerd, which in turn calls runc to do the lowest-level work of actually creating and starting the container process. This handoff chain is what the Docker Internals module covers in full detail.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784479583980-220895310.png
blocks.alt: The daemon delegates downward instead of doing it all itself

blocks.content: 5. runc Builds the Isolated Process

runc is where the Linux kernel features actually get used: it creates fresh namespaces (so the container gets its own view of processes, network, and filesystem) and applies cgroup limits (so it cannot exceed its allotted CPU or memory), then finally starts your application's process inside that sealed environment.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784479585539-940903571.png
blocks.alt: This is the exact moment isolation actually happens

blocks.content: 6. Putting the Whole Path Together

Every one of the previous steps chains into the next: CLI to daemon, daemon to registry only if needed, daemon to containerd, containerd to runc, and finally a running, isolated container process. Once you can trace this whole path from memory, you can reason about failures at any point along it, a pull failure, a permissions error, a resource limit, by knowing exactly which stage is responsible.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784479587283-18596506.png
blocks.alt: The complete path, start to finish

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A single docker run touches five distinct stages: client, daemon, registry (conditionally), containerd, and runc, in that exact order.
Knowing this chain by heart is what lets you diagnose exactly where a failure happened, instead of treating "docker run failed" as one big mystery.
